title: Keeping Cash Transactions in Australia Bill 2024
short_title: Keeping Cash Transactions in Australia Bill 2024

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: The bill would require businesses that sell goods or services to the public in person to offer cash as a payment option, and to take it, for transactions up to $10,000.
A business that refused cash would face a maximum civil penalty of $5,000 for an individual or $25,000 for a body corporate, enforced under Part 4 of the Regulatory Powers Act.
The duty would not apply where taking cash posed a reasonable security risk, breached another law or current official health advice, or where change was not readily available.
changes: Businesses supplying goods or services in person at a premises, or from a vehicle or structure, would have to offer and accept cash payment.
Payments above $10,000, or above any higher amount prescribed by rules, would be excluded from the requirement.
A contravention would attract a maximum civil penalty of $5,000 for an individual and $25,000 for a body corporate.
The bill would treat partnerships, unincorporated associations and trusts as if each were a person.
The Minister would be able to make rules prescribing matters the bill requires or permits.
The bill would commence the day after three months from Royal Assent and would extend to every external Territory.
summary.affected: Businesses that sell goods or services to the public in person, customers who pay in cash, and the Minister responsible for making rules are affected.

divisions.question: The majority voted against a motion introduced by Calare MP [Andrew Gee](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/representatives/calare/andrew_gee) (Independent), which means it failed. ### Motion text > *That so much of the standing and sessional orders be suspended as would prevent the following from occurring immediately:* > > *(1) the Member for Calare introducing the [Keeping Cash Transactions in Australia Bill](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/Bills_Search_Results/Result?bId=r7202); and* > > *(2) debate on the second reading of the bill proceeding for a period of no longer than one hour, after which any questions required to complete passage of the bill then being put without delay.* Standing and sessional orders are the usual procedural rules of parliament.
